### **1.  Introduction & Executive Summary** 

##### **1.1 Introduction** 

Silver enjoyed an extraordinary bull market in 2010 as the metal’s price hit a thirty-year high of $30.70 in late December.  This not only represented and intra-year increase of around 80% but that level was also more than three times the ‘low’ seen in late 2008.  What made silver’s gains even more impressive is its massive outperformance of gold in the final third of the year; then the gold:silver ratio fell sharply to below 50 by end-2010, a level last seen in early 2008. 

As with gold, the silver rally last year was mainly driven by strong investment inflows, which are estimated to have totalled $4.7 billion (up 60% yearon-year).  Looking at the reasons for this, first and foremost, silver benefited from the spill over from buoyant demand for gold as a

safe haven asset, chiefly as a result of negative short term real interest rates, the European sovereign debt crisis and growing fears over longer term inflation particularly after the ‘QE2’ announcement by the US Federal Reserve. In addition, as the silver market is less liquid and its price consequently more volatile than gold, it has become increasingly popular among more speculative players who often use silver for enhanced returns. Indeed, there was evidence of higher prices spurring trendfollowing silver purchases in the final quarter of 2010. Silver’s price rise last year, however, was not just an investment story. Of great importance was the 74 Moz rebound in industrial demand (and it was frequently observed that silver took strength from positive news on the outlook for industrial metals). Although we are generally bullish about the silver price in 2011, we would caution some potential downside risk, due to the metal’s historically high volatility coupled with ongoing uncertainties over the world economy.  With regards to that, the impressive rally seen in both the commodity and equity markets yearto-date has been primarily driven by upbeat economic statistics, mainly from the United States. 

However, we believe that the current positive sentiment over economic growth in western economies this year seems to be somewhat excessive, as the unemployment rate is still at elevated levels and consumer confidence remains fragile.  Indeed, as explained in detail in Chapter 2, we expect sluggish world GDP growth of 2.8% this year compared to 4.0% in 2010.  As such, it is very likely that the commodity and equity markets could see a major sell-off if investor sentiment changes and momentum falters.  Having said that, we expect any correction to be temporary and short-lived, because bargain hunting could emerge, be that from investors or industrial fabricators. 

Looking further ahead, while economic conditions are forecast to eventually stabilise in 2012, central banks in most advanced economies will be reluctant to raise interest rates in order to avoid damaging market confidence.  Therefore, silver prices should remain at high levels, with investment demand only starting to weaken in the second half of next year, taking the annual average price to $30.69.  Thereafter, as inflation continues to rise in 2013, we would expect some substantial interest rate hikes that year which will then reduce silver’s appeal as a safe haven asset. Nevertheless, the absolute level of investment demand should remain historically high.  This suggests that prices can be maintained above $25 for much of 2013 to reach an annual average of $25.28 in that year. 

We can also project two potential scenarios for the global economy very different to our Base Case.

This is basis a secular recovery in the dollar and a low level of inflation, reflecting governments’ failure to boost private demand and consumer spending in advanced economies. As mentioned previously, however, we do not subscribe to the view that price direction and level are determined by investment alone. An analysis of trends in the key supply/demand variables shows that these have had and will continue to play an important part in price

##### **1.2 Base Case Scenario** 

Looking at the supply side, **mine production** is expected to maintain healthy growth over the next three years, resulting in successive record highs.  The forecast is premised on an expansion in all sectors of silver output, as new projects come on stream and lives of existing operations are extended.  Moreover, the ongoing improvement in world economic growth should enhance producers’ ability to raise finance.  This plus silver’s strong price performance should give an additional boost to market confidence, which will in turn push production higher.  It is general positives such as these that led us to raise the forecast in each year by around 10 Moz since the November report. 

In contrast and despite a rising price, silver **scrap** is likely to fall from 2011 onwards, mainly due to the ongoing structural decline in photographic scrap. Jewellery and silverware scrap are also forecast to fall but only from 2012, as this year sees a noticeable price-led increase.  Industrial scrap in contrast should track broadly sideways out to 2013 as underlying growth factors balance out the impact of a falling price. Our total scrap figures have also been raised slightly since November due in the main to higher prices. 

**Net government sales** are set to fall over the next two years and remain subdued thereafter, with its contribution to total supply falling below 1% by 2013 (an outlook unchanged on our previous report). 

It is important to point out a major change in our forecast for **producer hedging** .  In our November report, we forecast slight net de-hedging in 2010 (and a broadly neutral situation thereafter) but our revised figure for last year shows a return to net hedging (of some 29.5 Moz), an outcome last seen in 2005.  This swing was primarily due to the recently listed Minera Frisco which, in late 2010, hedged 70.1 Moz out to 2013.  Tied in with those actions, we now expect yet greater hedging in 2011, with by-product producers the chief practitioners.  Thereafter, as prices start to ease in 









the second half of 2012, we expect a fall in net hedging that year before net _de-_ hedging re-emerges in 2013. 

As for demand, **total fabrication** is forecast to rise by almost 100 Moz between 2010 and 2013, with the **industrial** sector accounting for the vast bulk of these gains.  Last year, industrial offtake is estimated to have risen by 20% from a six-year low in 2009 due to stock replenishment, the emergence of pent-up demand and a return to positive economic growth.  With ongoing GDP gains, industrial demand should continue to rise out to 2013.  However, as the restocking process was almost complete by end-2010, the pace of forecast increases will be slower than last year, particularly in 2011 due to the uncertainties in many western economies.  Since November, our industrial offtake estimates have been raised in each year by around 20 Mo

z, reflecting the lift to our GDP forecasts and highlighting short to medium term price inelasticity. 

**Jewellery** demand is also forecast to post increases in each year from 2011 to 2013, albeit on a far smaller scale.  This higher offtake is mainly a result of heavy substitution gains from gold jewellery, although better economic conditions particularly in western markets and further penetration of silver jewellery in Asian countries are also important to the outcome.  Higher prices, however, are expected to dent **silverware** offtake this year but the subsequent price retreat is not likely to usher in a recovery as that is countered by negative structural factors, giving a fairly stable demand profile.  There is unlikely to be any priceled respite for **photography** as its digitally-driven structural downtrend continues relentlessly out to 2013. 

Lastly, demand for **coins & medals** is set to rise this year, reflecting general growing investor interest in silver.  As investment then starts to wane from 2012 onwards, coin demand should also fall but it is expected to remain at historically high levels in all years.  Our estimates for coins, jewellery and silverware have all been raised slightly since the November report. 

Overall, the supply and demand figures forecast show that the market will remain in surplus (as defined by the sum of mine production plus scrap less fabrication) over the next three years, which suggests that the silver price is vulnerable to a major correction. Nevertheless, given that the economic backdrop will remain generally favourable for investment demand for silver, we expect investors to fairly comfortably absorb the surplus metal over the forecast period.

##### **1.3 Alternative Scenarios** 

The bullish **Scenario B** , with a price rising above $50 at its peak in the final year of the forecast, is expected to see major gains in investment due to a weaker dollar and a pick-up in inflation.  At $13.2 billion in 2013, World Investment’s value is around 180% higher than in 2010 and triple the Base Case figure. 

Not surprisingly, these higher forecast prices result in major differences between Scenario B’s supply/demand balance and that for the Base Case.  First, the rise in prices will spur a notably greater level of supply, chiefly as a result of higher growth in mine output, successive gains in scrap and more aggressive producer hedging, particularly in 2012 and 2013.  As regards the latter, we expect more diversified producers to become enticed into securing bountiful non-core silver revenue due to that metal’s markedly higher prices. 

As for demand, industrial offtake should see more rapid gains than in the Base Case given faster GDP growth.  There should also be a marked investment driven rise in coin fabrication and even jewellery still manages gains, mainly courtesy of substitutio

n from gold. Even with structural losses in silverware and photography, total fabrication in 2013 could be almost 160 Moz higher than in 2010. Changes since November mainly comprise markedly higher producer hedging and notably greater mine production and industrial offtake. Under **Scenario C** , the silver price is expected to start a steady fall later this year, with the annual average falling by 35% or $8 in the final two years of the forecast. Key to this is a decline in investor interest, with World Investment forecast to fall by 26% and 19% in 2012 and 2013 respectively to around 153 Moz in the final year (12% below our Base Case figure in tonnage terms and a dramatic 48% lower in value terms). Although this investor-led bear market does see a hefty decline in prices, the outcome would be far worse if it were not for the support which is expected to emerge from other supply/demand developments over the period. For example, growth in total supply will be very limited compared to the Base Case, given a less robust increase in mine production, a sharp decline in scrap and less producer hedging activity. Turning to fabrication demand, despite lower world GDP growth, industrial demand for silver will continue to rise, albeit at a slower pace, while lower prices should result in higher demand for jewellery and to a degree silverware. As such, total fabrication less coins is estimated at only 20-25 Moz below the Base Case in each forecast year. Despite more muted supply, the market surplus will be larger than under the Base Case, with bargain hunting investors therefore being expected to help absorb the surplus. Price & Economic Assumptions** ##### **2.1 Introduction** GFMS’ views for the forecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, namely the Base Case Scenario, Scenario B and Scenario C. Under our Base

Case projections we expect a slowdown in global GDP growth this year, partly as the effect of fiscal stimulus plans ebb, before a gradual pick up in growth occurs over the final two years of our forecast due to improvements in the underlying world economy. We view this as the most likely scenario and since our November forecast the probability of our Base Case Scenario has remained at 50%. Our more bullish Scenario B, to which we assign a 30% probability, predicts inflation rising over the next three years, albeit modestly at first, above all in the United States. Central to this scenario are the policies being followed by the US government and the Federal Reserve. These include a continuation of the very loose fiscal and monetary policy including the second round of quantitative easing. Such policies are forecast to largely avert a renewed economic slowdown in 201113 but at the cost of rising inflation, with it reaching an annual average of 5.5% in 2013. Moreover, the US dollar weakens under this scenario. Under our bearish Scenario C, to which we assign a 20% probability, we expect the effect of government measures to be negligible on the longer run growth rate as the global economy struggles to escape deflation. Consequently, global GDP growth slows appreciably in 2011 and remains sluggish over much of the rest of the forecast period, particularly in the developed world. We then discuss in more detail each of the three economic scenarios and, finally, comment on what impact each of these could have on silver prices between now and the end of 2013 ##### **2.2 Economic Backdrop** In 2010 global growth recovered faster than we had anticipated considering the underlying structural problems of many economies. Accordingly, we now estimate world GDP growth to have been 4.1% in 2010, up from 3.7% in our November forecast. However, there are signs that the slower growth we had forecast to take place is starting to occur now, although more modestly than we had anticipated. In the developing world this is attributable to attempts to moderate the growth rates in their economies in an attempt to quell inflat
